body: “Besides, Carmen has something that neither an aqueduct nor a cathedral has, and that is that when we look at you, we see ourselves. Today, Carmen, as you go up to collect this award, you carry inside you all those women you have portrayed from the beginning: Your mother, your aunts and your neighbors accompany you.”

Machi also starred in “Celeste,” created by San José, which won her best actress as well as best series at Series Mania’s International Panorama last year. Superb in Carlota Pereda’s Sundance hit “Piggy,” Machi has demonstrated her chops for drama and melodrama, incarnating the oldest version of a heinously messianic mother in “La Mesías,” from Javier Ambrossi and Javirr Calvo, now behind “La Bola Negra.”

articles.title: Miley’s ‘Bass Persuades’ Is Pretty and Passable, but Surprisingly Light on Bass… or Persuasion: Album Review
articles.summary: The title track and first single from Miley Cyrus’ “Bass Persuades” was a classic act of misdirection, we now learn. Released two and a half weeks prior to the album, the song promised a tenth album full of bangers (with an S or Z, take your pick), mildly scolding the young people for not being
body: The core message of the album seems to be that things are going pretty well — make that extremely well — with fiancée Maxx Morando, who is a writer-producer collaborator on all but two of the tracks. Hearing Miley in a besotted state turns up mixed results. The third track, “Let’s Get Married,” is an abrupt left turn from the two bang-ier numbers that precede it into synthy easy listening/AC flavors, and what it delivers is not worth the whiplash; while it will probably be heard at some weddings to come, there may be a lot of attendees who would be itchy to please skip ahead to the vows.

Fortunately, that syrupy aside is a low point from which the album fairly quickly recovers. “Orbit,” next up, is just as romantic but one of the collection’s better tracks, as a power ballad — or even just ballad, without so much emphasis on the power — that applies some clever turns of phrase and thought to what could be a tired metaphor. Her significant other is the center of her solar system: “Place a marble on the floor / When you walk in the room, it’ll roll to you” is an image that makes for a lovely mash note.

articles.title: Amanda Redman: ‘My most embarrassing moment? Getting caught doing a pretend Bafta thank you speech’
articles.summary: The actor on a terrible accident as a toddler, her bossy nature, and feeling too old to play a Shakespearean heroine. Born in Brighton, Amanda Redman, 69, studied at Bristol Old Vic theatre school. She starred in the TV comedy drama El C.I.D.
body: When were you happiest? I am happiest when I have my daughter and granddaughter with me.

What is your earliest memory? Being in hospital. I was standing up in a cot and we were being asked what we wanted for lunch. I think it was Great Ormond Street. I had managed to pull a cauldron of boiling turkey and vegetable soup all over me when I was 18 months old, and I spent five years of my life in various hospitals.
Which living person do you most admire and why? Barack Obama, for his decency. I felt real hope when he was elected, which has been dashed now.
What is the trait you most deplore in others? Meanness of spirit.

articles.title: TIFF 2026: Primetime Program Spotlights Upcoming TV Hits
articles.summary: As one of the first festivals to have a slate dedicated solely to television, the 11th year of the Toronto International Film Festival’s Primetime slate is the most expansive it’s ever been.
body: Primetime’s 2026 slate was the program’s most expansive yet, so without further ado, here are the highlights.

Netflix’s “Below” follows Calvin Penney (Josh Hartnett), a widower and father whose ice harvesting job is being sabotaged by contaminated ice. Traumatized by his father’s death when he was a child when his family was forced to relocate their home, his memories begin to rear their ugly head as two of his three children come back to visit during a “Come Home Year,” where previous residents are encouraged to return to their hometown. While this homecoming reunites the entire family for the first time in years, it also gives way to a darkness that none of them are prepared to confront, uncovering interesting threads concerning assimilation and, of course, climate change.

articles.title: ‘He’s simply astonishing’: will Andrew Scott become the first out gay man to win the best actor Oscar?
articles.summary: The Irishman seems a dead cert for his performance as Ian Charleson in Elsinore. And his ability to avoid being pigeonholed while embracing queer stories, from Pride to All of Us Strangers, is a remarkable achievement.
body: This Sunday, the curtain falls on the Toronto film festival, the last of the three big autumn showcases – alongside Venice and Telluride – that are launchpads for award campaigns. And as the dust settles on the red carpets, one name rises above the others as destined for sure-fire glory: Andrew Scott.

The Irish actor, 50 next month, is now not only considered a lock for a leading actor Oscar nomination but almost certain to take the prize next spring. Should he win, he will become the first out gay actor to do so in the Academy’s almost 100-year history.

If that’s a fact that seems astonishing today, it would have felt an inevitability in 1989, when the film for which Scott has been so praised is set. In Elsinore, he plays Ian Charleson, the dashing Scottish star of films including Chariots of Fire and Gandhi. Charleson had been given his first role three years before Chariots by Derek Jarman, but excised it from his CV (leading to a lifelong rift, depicted in Elsinore). Muting his sexuality was then considered essential in the pursuit of stardom. Yet despite such curation – and his undeniable talents – Charleson never reached the level of fame he felt he deserved.

Then, in the Sala Grande, the main screening hall of the Venice film festival within the Palazzo del Cinema, the audience stood almost as…
body: The film the audience had watched for 80 harrowing minutes was the Gaza documentary NAZA, which has been produced by the Guardian.
The film’s title comes from an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically to refer to the civilians expected to be killed in a military attack.

Unfolding against the background of Tel Aviv at night, the participants – intelligence officers and other soldiers – describe a series of systems, some powered by AI, that select the thousands who should die in strikes, often at night and surrounded by their families.
Perhaps most challenging for Israel’s political elite is that it is a story told exclusively in Hebrew by 24 anonymised Israeli military insiders, many of them from elite units.

articles.title: CA Gov. Gavin Newsom Signs Bill Addressing Catch in $750M Tax Credit for Hollywood
articles.summary: The new law exempts indie projects from caps on the use of state tax credits and offers productions enhanced monetization of their incentives.
body: California Gov. Gavin Newsom on Friday signed into law a bill aimed at reducing Hollywood’s exposure to recent business tax credit caps legislation.

In a visit to Warner Bros. Studios the governor gave the green light to SB 186, which exempts independent productions from caps on the use of state tax credits that this year were not only extended, but also rendered permanent as of 2030.

SB 186 additionally offers new perks for productions that choose to monetize their tax credits instead of applying them to their annual tax bill: Productions can now monetize 95 percent of the credits instead of the previous 90 percent. Their payout timeline is also sped up to two years instead of the previous five.

It’s not a full exemption for Hollywood, but it’s a change that the industry pushed hard for. “Today’s action will maintain the state’s competitiveness so creators continue to make movies and shows in California — and keep bringing brilliant stories to life,” Motion Picture Association vp of state government affairs Arlen Valdivia said in a statement. “We thank Governor Newsom for his continued support for our industry’s health.”

articles.title: John Wilson on his unlikely concrete movie: ‘There might be a kind of sickness in shooting things this way’
articles.summary: The creator of How To with John Wilson has returned with his first film, a documentary about how to sell a documentary about concrete. As mayor of New York City, Zohran Mamdani has frequently demonstrated impressive media savvy, but arguably nothing has proved his genius for in-the-know promo more…
body: It was because of that scaffolding episode, released in October 2020, that I, like some smart Mamdani staffers, began to perceive the sidewalk shed shadowing my block not as an inevitable fixed entity but an obtrusive, if well-intentioned, symptom of neglect. Shortly after the mayor’s video, said scaffolding miraculously came down – revealing, to my shock, a three square-wide swath of concrete that had not seen the sun in six years.

When I credit Wilson for this upgrade, in person at a film office in Manhattan, he reacts with a modest “I’ll take it,” as dry as the dusty footprints of the recently departed metal poles. Fitting, for though that newly revealed concrete, speckled with old gum and anonymous residue, is certainly better, if not exactly beautiful, perhaps only Wilson could see it as cinematic. His debut feature film, The History of Concrete, takes on the granddaddy of all urban materials, tugging wry insights on our terminal human condition out of the crumbling facades of New York’s most pervasive substance.

articles.title: This Cozy Western Series Streaming On Netflix Is A Comforting Watch
articles.summary: If you're looking for a Western series without the intensity and violence of Taylor Sheridan's work, you may watch to catch this show on Netflix.
body: In the wake of what can only be described as an onslaught of Taylor Sheridan shows, Western entertainment is enjoying a renaissance. We've had everything from straight-up "Yellowstone" clones to Western versions of "The Summer I Turned Pretty" (check out the underrated Netflix show "My Life with the Walter Boys" if you're intrigued). Now, there's more: Netflix just added an extremely cozy little Hallmark series that's perfect for Western fans who are also partial to a little small town Canadian romance.

Created by Alfonso H. Moreno, "When Hope Calls" is actually a spin-off from the show "When Calls the Heart," on which Moreno served as showrunner. That Hallmark Western romantic drama is, in turn, based on Janette Oke's six-book "Canadian West" series and has been running for an incredible 13 seasons, with a 14th set to debut in 2027. "When Hope Calls," debuted as an offshoot of "When Calls the Heart" back in August 2019, originally running on the streaming service Hallmark Movies Now before being aired on Hallmark Channel starting in 2020.
